newsitem.title: USA: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. trade gap $11.34 bln in Sept.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - U.S. trade gap $11.34 bln in Sept.

text.p: Following are comments from U.S. economists after the Commerce Department reported the September trade gap swelled to $11.34 billion compared to a revised $10.30 billion the prior month.
Experts had expected a $9.5 billion deficit.
DONALD MAUDE, CHIEF U.S. ECONOMIST, SCOTIA CAPITAL MARKETS INC: "It's surprising because the Commerce Department estimated exports would have been up. They were down 1.4 (percent).

"Imports, they were expecting to be flat, which it was. This will probably shave about two-tenths off of third-quarter GDP. Maybe even three-tenths. I'm looking for about a 1.7 (percent) third-quarter GDP, versus 2.2 (percent in Q2).

"China has definitely surpassed Japan as the highest deficit country. This is going to cause some political rumblings, because we already have representatives over there right now and it's very contentious.
"You're going to hear a lot of talk from Congress about China. The 'Most Favored Nation' trade status may come up for debate again," Maude added.
ASTRID ADOLFSON, FIRST VICE PRESIDENT AND SENIOR ECONOMIST, MCM MONEYWATCH INC: "Surprising numbers to say the least ... most people were expecting the reverse.
"Aircraft was the problem. Aircraft exports plunged, so that was really the reason why exports were so weak."

SALLY KLEINMAN, ECONOMIST, CHASE SECURITIES INC: "Clearly, it was much worse than anticipated. It does not help solve the mystery of missing inventories, which the Commerce overstates in third quarter (Gross Domestic Product). It means that they'll lower GDP by some amount ..."

LEE YOUNGDAHL, BOND MARKET ANALYST, AUBREY G. LANSTON & CO INC: "The export side was very bad with a decline of over 0.1 percent versus an expected rise, and it was really based across major categories. You may get some comeback in the months ahead, but clearly the dollar's strength earlier this year and sluggishness of recovery abroad is weighing on exports. Overall, it points to a downward revision to third quarter GDP ... when you take in other factors, you might not get too much of a change, but you might get a 2.0 percent print for example. Going forward, it points out that the U.S. dollar might have seen its best days in the near term."
ELLIOTT PLATT, MANAGING DIRECTOR OF ECONOMIC RESEARCH, DONALDSON, LUFKIN & JENRETTE SECURITIES CORP: "A major surprise ... everybody expected numbers to be down significantly.

"The entire decline and deterioration in the trade deficit was due to a sharp decline in exports particularly exports of capital goods ... it dropped by close to about one billion dollars. I think the decline in exports probably reflects the weakness in the European and Japanese economies," Platt added.

GARY THAYER, SENIOR ECONOMIST, A.G. EDWARDS & SONS INC: "This suggests the dollar is getting to a pricey level overall. While we've seen trade deficits widening while the dollar was strenghtening, we may now be at a point where higher trade deficit numbers are going to weigh on the dollar.

"Some of the increase in the trade deficit is due to higher energy prices. We are now heading into the winter with seasonally strong demand, so this factor could also boost the trade deficit numbers through the spring.
"A bigger deficit, coupled with stronger foreign economies in Europe, could put downward pressure on the dollar," he said.
Thayer continued: "We are looking for the dollar to weaken over the next three to six months.
"This could put more upward pressure on inflation in the U.S."

WILLIAM SULLIVAN, DIRECTOR OF MONEY MARKET RESEARCH, DEAN WITTER REYNOLDS INC: "You see a significant rewidening in the overall gap for the month of September. In fact, it is more than a billion above the revised deficit for October. It's a by-product of some renewed weakness in exports ... and a good share represented a significant downturn in aircraft shipments," he added.

Sullivan continued: "Meanwhile, imports held in at high levels. They actually rose one-tenth to 80.13 billion and part of that reflected higher energy prices and a bigger energy trade gap in general. So clearly, this is the type of figure that may result in a downward revision to real GDP."
-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1660
